items.body: German multi-instrumentalist Udo Schindler has been recording and releasing music relentlessly over the last few years. The reviews below offer a glimpse of just some of his production over the first half of this year. Udo Schindler and Elisabeth Harnik – Poetry of Friction (arch-musik, 2026) To his immense credit, architect of buildings (by day) and sounds (by night) Udo Schindler is tireless and itinerant. He has some of core collaborators – see Harald Kimmig and Eric Zwang Eriksson on Imprints of Experiences below – but, more often, he pushes his music forward by performing with new musicians. Presumably, this forces him and his collaborators to adapt to each other on the spot, and in the process explore unanticipated sonic territories. Poetry of Friction captures Schindler on tenor sax, clarinet, and cornet in a duo with Elisabeth Harnik on Bechstein piano (in and out) at a May 2025 performance at Musik- & Pianohaus Schwinghammer in Weilheim in Oberbayern, Germany. The affair is largely muted. Both Harnik and Schindler have been studying extended techniques and uncustomary articulations for years, and as should be of no surprise given the title, they continue to do so here, focusing on frictions, burbles, and heavy vibrations rather than anything crisp or ostensibly melodic. If one were to consider this a duel, Schindler has found his match in Harnik, who just as adeptly swings from idiomatic to non-idiomatic techniques. Some passages are blustery and beautiful. Some are hardly audible, roughly textured flutters and other understated soundscaping. Whichever way the duo veers, however, Schindler and Harnik stay linked and measured, wandering wide spaces but most often in tandem, which finds an unexpected potential in the soulful and dramatic climax and release of its final minutes. Poetry of Friction is available as a download on Bandcamp. Poetry of Friction by Udo Schindler & Elisabeth Harnik Udo Schindler and Sergio Armaroli – Transalpine Sound Bridges (Munich-Milan) (Fundacja Słuchaj, 2026) Transalpine Sound Bridges is the oddball of the group. Whereas the other releases were recorded live in studio or in front of an audience, this album came out of a canceled duo gig. As no in person collaboration had (or has yet) taken place, Sergio Armaroli responded by recording a series of vibraphone and percussion solos for Schindler (soprano sax, clarinets, flute, cornet) to improvise over. The result is a music that wafts through space. As the other releases here attest, Schindler can honk, contort, and scream with the best of them. Here, likely inspired by Armaroli’s dreamy runs on the vibraphone, Schindler also shows that he can lean into minimalist, calmer motifs. One hears his expert control, but in restraint rather than this John Butcher-like acrobatics. This album reflects on some remote Alpine mountain range rather than conquering the Großglockner’s peak. In a sense, this is impressionist more than expressionist, which is notable given the improvisations have taken place remotely. It grapples with that tension in the colorful patchworks of yielding and unyielding pastures, unsteady breezes, a panorama of beautiful flowers juxtaposed to barren crags, peace with a soft undertone or playful danger. Consider Transalpine Sound Bridges yet another side of Schindler that ranges from the bucolic and airy to the positively bluesy, coaxed in those directions by Armaroli’s knottily vining solo chasses and the vagaries of circumstance. Available as a double CD and download from bandcamp. Transalpine Sound Bridges [Munich-Milano] 2CD by Udo Schindler & Sergio Armaroli Udo Schindler and Uwe Oberg – Schädel-Magie (FMR, 2026) The title, Schädel-Magie , is German for skull magic, which sounds quite macabre. But maybe we should think of it in terms of sounds bouncing around the inner caverns of the head, in the eardrums and the auditory cortex and amygdala, rather than something more sinister. The skull in this analogy is self-evident, and the magic lay in the music produced, received, and processed. (A quick internet search tells me sound processing is an extremely complicated and weird, and in that sense quasi-magical, process, as much higher brain functioning is.) The album, Schädel-Magie, features Schindler on various clarinets and alto flute, and Uwe Oberg on piano (like Harnik, in and out) and captures the duo in studio in 2024. The track titles are untranslatable (or nonsensical?) compound nouns invented by the late German poet Thomas Kling. If the words themselves do not quite carry over into English (what the hell is a body-branch or night machine?) the collectivity of the sounds are universal and perform a universal linguo-emotive magic of their own. Schädel-Magie begins as a wild and winding romp but quickly dissipates into extended passages of piano and saxophone constructivism. From there, Schindler and Oberg shift into a series of noirish pieces that explore a range of techniques and dynamics, though always drawn to some dark, mysterious corner. Or a winding staircase at the darkest part of night, wherein nothing nefarious has to happen but various anxious potentialities nevertheless reside in its shadows. As much as anything else, Schädel-Magie distinguishes itself from the other albums reviewed here in its mood – even in its tender moments one senses something cryptic, if not also haunting – and its barbed-wire spiraling. Schädel-Magie is available via the arc-musik website: https://arch-musik.de/project/schaedel-magie/ . Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.excerpt: プログレッシヴなR&Bを歌うリヴ（Liv.e）と奇才ドラマーのカリーム・リギンスが組んだユニット。ダラスとデトロイトの出身者で奏でるネオ・ソウル由来のビート・ミュージックは、エリカ・バドゥと故J・ディラのコラボも連想させる。が、即興性の高いローファイで不定形な楽曲はジャズやファンクをベースにしながらも既存のジャンルを飛び越え、〈オルタナティヴ〉という言葉さえ生温い。アイザイア・シャーキーのギターを交えてプリンスの如く疾走すれば、ジェイムズ・フランシーズのメロウな鍵盤と亡霊のようなコーラスで妖しく迫るなど、カラフルな音使いでダークなトーンにまとめ上げた怪作だ。

items.body:
Before getting into the controversy, Massive Attack’s Singapore concert on 29 July was, in this writer’s opinion, far and away the best show the country has seen this year. It was transcendent, thought-provoking and deeply moving — the kind of performance that reminded you what live music can achieve when sound, visuals, politics, and emotion come together with absolute purpose.

The British trip-hop pioneers did not simply play a collection of songs. They built an overwhelming audiovisual experience that felt urgent, unsettling, and profoundly human. And yet, one of the biggest conversations to emerge from the night has not been about the concert itself. Instead, it has been about a flag.

Near the end of the performance at The Star Theatre, Massive Attack members Robert “3D” Del Naja and Grant “Daddy G” Marshall held up a Palestinian flag as the audience cheered. Del Naja then said “Free Palestine”, after which members of the crowd independently took up the chant.

In the days after the show, Singapore Police confirmed that reports had been lodged and investigations were ongoing. The Infocomm Media Development Authority also said it was investigating a possible breach of the concert’s licence conditions.

Concert promoter Lushington Entertainments said it was aware of the reports and would “fully cooperate with the relevant authorities as required”.

The band also told the audience that it had removed a song from its setlist because of “local laws”, although it did not elaborate further. At the time of writing, the authorities have not confirmed which song was omitted or why.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Adele Chan 🇸🇬 (@adele__chan)

For readers unfamiliar with the controversy, Singapore does not allow the public display of foreign national emblems without a permit or exemption. Those convicted of doing so may face a fine of up to S$500, imprisonment of up to six months, or both.

That explains why the authorities have the power to investigate the incident. It does not make the situation any less ridiculous. There was no reported violence. No threat to the audience. No indication that the concert became unsafe. Two musicians held up a flag, members of the crowd cheered, and the show came to an end.

Yet somewhere between the stage lights going down and everyone heading home, the moment became a police and regulatory matter. Massive Attack raised a Palestinian flag. Singapore raised an investigation. Only here could an expression of solidarity generate this much paperwork.

To be clear, visiting artists are not exempt from local laws. Musicians, promoters, and venues are expected to comply with the conditions attached to their performances, whether or not they personally agree with them. But legality and proportionality are not the same thing. A regulation may provide grounds for an investigation without making that investigation sensible, necessary, or remotely proportionate to what actually happened. Context should matter.

Massive Attack were not encouraging violence. They were not promoting an armed organisation. They were not placing the audience in danger or transforming the venue into an unsafe environment. They displayed a flag associated with the Palestinian people and voiced their support for Palestinian freedom. A Palestinian flag is not the flag of Hamas. Support for Palestinian civilians, dignity, freedom, or statehood should not automatically be treated as a threat to public order.

Yet the official response risks blurring that distinction. It turns a brief gesture of solidarity into something suspicious enough to warrant police reports, licensing scrutiny, and the possibility of criminal penalties. And for what?

The audience saw the flag. Some concertgoers cheered. Others may have disagreed. The country did not descend into chaos. The performance ended. Singapore remained standing. The political nature of the gesture should not have surprised anyone either.

Massive Attack have spent decades incorporating questions of war, state power, surveillance, inequality, and human rights into their work. Their politics are not an inconvenient addition to their music. They are woven into the group’s identity and creative output.

In 2025, the band also helped establish a collective supporting musicians who had spoken out about Israel’s military actions in Gaza, alleging that artists faced intimidation and pressure within the music industry for doing so. Political expression is not an unexpected interruption at a Massive Attack concert. It is part of the concert.

Fans do not attend their shows expecting the uncomfortable parts of the world to be neatly edited out. They go knowing the group has something to say and that the performance may ask more of them than passive enjoyment. That does not mean every audience member must agree with the band. It means artists should be able to articulate a position without every uncomfortable gesture being escalated into a potential public-order issue.

Singaporeans often joke that complaining is a national pastime. Something happens. Someone takes offence. A report gets filed. Suddenly, a moment that might otherwise have passed becomes an official matter requiring statements, investigations, and administrative attention.

That instinct can be useful when genuine harm has occurred. But not every source of discomfort is dangerous. Not every disagreement demands intervention. And not everything that happens on a concert stage needs to become a police report. The urge to complain about anything remotely contentious can produce a society that is orderly but increasingly unable to distinguish between actual harm and simple unease. A flag may make some people uncomfortable. Discomfort is not disorder.

There is also a wider concern for Singapore’s live music scene. The country has worked hard to establish itself as a major touring destination in Asia. International artists, promoters, and fans increasingly view Singapore as a reliable stop for arena concerts, theatre performances, and large-scale cultural events.

But a thriving concert ecosystem cannot be built solely on efficient venues, clean facilities, and orderly crowds. It also requires space for artists to be artists. Music has never existed outside politics. From protest songs and benefit concerts to stage speeches and visual statements, musicians have always used live performance to respond to the world around them.

Audiences are capable of encountering those ideas. They can applaud, disagree, remain silent, walk away, or argue about them after the lights come on. That exchange is part of what gives live music its meaning. It is not disorder. It is culture.

That was especially evident during Massive Attack’s performance. The show was moving precisely because it refused to separate art from the world that produced it. Its visuals, music, and messages worked together to confront the audience with questions of violence, power, and human suffering. Removing that political dimension would not have made the concert more neutral. It would have made it less honest.

The authorities will determine whether Massive Attack breached the conditions attached to their performance licence. But the public is equally entitled to ask whether an alleged breach deserved this degree of scrutiny in the first place. A Palestinian flag appeared at a concert. It did not place the audience in danger. It did not threaten Singapore’s stability. It did not require a national demonstration of bureaucratic efficiency.

Perhaps, instead of rushing to complain, report, and investigate, we could acknowledge the moment for what it was: a political gesture by an openly political band during one of the most remarkable concerts Singapore has hosted this year. Massive Attack raised a flag. The crowd responded. The music continued. Perhaps we should have simply allowed the moment to speak for itself.

PREP are heading back to Asia! The London indie-pop quartet have announced a new run of headline shows across the region in support of their latest EP, One Day In The Sun, bringing their signature blend of sophisticated pop, smooth grooves, and nostalgic melodies to fans across seven cities.

Kicking off on 2 October, the tour will see the band perform in Taipei, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Kuala Lumpur, Manila, and Bangkok, while also making a special appearance at the Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix. Fans can expect a setlist featuring favourites from PREP's catalogue alongside tracks from One Day In The Sun, including music from their recent collaboration with Taiwanese indie outfit Sunset Rollercoaster.

The upcoming run marks another milestone for the band, whose following across East and Southeast Asia has continued to grow over the past decade. PREP previously sold out multiple shows across the region during their 2024 Asia tour and have also performed at festivals including VERY Festival in Thailand, Clockenflap in Hong Kong, and Seoul Jazz Festival.

Known for their polished musicianship and laid-back live performances, PREP have amassed more than 650 million streams across digital platforms. Southeast Asia remains one of the band's strongest markets, with Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines, Malaysia, and Taiwan among their biggest global audiences. Their cover of Harry Styles' 'As It Was' has also become a viral hit online, racking up billions of views across social media.

items.body:
SB19 have officially etched their names into music history. On 31 July, the five-piece became the first-ever P-pop act to perform at Lollapalooza, taking over the Allianz Stage in Chicago with a high-energy 10-song set that marked another milestone for Filipino music on the global festival circuit.

Opening with 'DAM', the group powered through fan favourites including 'GENTO', 'Lawless', 'Emoji', 'MAPA', 'Wakas', 'Visa', 'Dungka!', and 'Crimzone'. They also gave audiences an exclusive preview of 'Mga Kababayan', their rendition of the late Francis Magalona classic, which is set to appear on the soundtrack of DreamWorks Animation's upcoming film Forgotten Island.

One of the biggest moments of the set came during 'Dungka!', when Chicago Bulls mascot Benny the Bull surprised fans by joining SB19 onstage, adding a distinctly Chicago touch to the group's landmark festival debut.

Following the performance, the quintet shared their gratitude with fans, writing: "What an unforgettable experience! We hope we made an impact, and we're beyond proud to represent the Philippines at Lollapalooza. Maraming salamat."

Rather than arriving at Lollapalooza in isolation, SB19's festival debut capped off one of the biggest weeks of the group's international career to date.

Ahead of the landmark performance, the quintet took the stage at the GRAMMY Museum's Global Spin Live in Los Angeles, where they performed 'GENTO' and 'Wakas' before taking part in a Q&A session about their journey and mission to bring Filipino music to the world.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by SB19 Official (@officialsb19)

Reflecting on the evening, the group shared, "The GRAMMY Museum gave us more than a stage. It gave us another reason to keep dreaming bigger. Last night was proof that our journey continues and that our mission to bring Filipino music to the world is far from over."

The milestones continued in Chicago, where member Josh represented the group by throwing the ceremonial first pitch before the Chicago White Sox's game against the New York Yankees. The appearance made SB19 the first Filipino group to receive the honour at a Major League Baseball game, adding yet another international first to their growing list of achievements.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by SB19 Official (@officialsb19)

Back home, the celebrations unfolded alongside the performance as thousands of A'TIN gathered for organised livestream watch parties across the Philippines. Hundreds of fans turned up before dawn at the Department of Tourism's free public screening at Rizal Park in Manila, while additional viewing events in Pampanga, Bacolod, Davao, Pasig, Cebu, and Cagayan de Oro transformed the early morning broadcast into a nationwide celebration.

The performance was also streamed globally via Disney+ and Weverse, while demand for local fan events remained high. Puregold's exclusive "A'TIN A'TIN Lang" watch party reportedly filled all 300 slots in under 30 minutes.

The celebrations are far from over. SB19 will next head to Japan for their I WaS There Thanksgiving Fan Meet at KT Zepp Yokohama before making another major festival appearance at Summer Sonic 2026, where they'll perform at both the Osaka and Tokyo editions on 14 and 15 August.

With their Lollapalooza debut now in the books, SB19 have delivered more than a historic first—they've capped off a remarkable week that saw the group perform on the Grammy Museum stage, step onto an MLB field, and introduce P-pop to one of the world's biggest music festivals, further cementing Filipino artists' growing presence on the global stage.

As Singapore's summer party season rolls on, MARQUEE Singapore keeps the momentum alive at Marina Bay Sands with another blockbuster lineup of global dance music heavyweights. From hardstyle and psytrance powerhouses to melodic storytellers and festival icons, August is packed with unforgettable nights that span every corner of the electronic music spectrum.

The month kicks off on Saturday, 8 August, as Australian-born producer Dimatik brings his signature blend of hardstyle and psytrance to the decks. With more than two million monthly Spotify listeners and support from the likes of Armin van Buuren, Tiësto, David Guetta, and Hardwell, Dimatik has become one of the scene's fastest-rising names. Behind massive tracks including 'Chamunda', 'Church of Hell', and the 150-million-stream hit 'Punjabi' with Timmy Trumpet, he arrives fresh from global festival appearances at Tomorrowland, Ultra Music Festival, and Knockout Outdoor, ready to unleash a barrage of high-BPM anthems and unreleased weapons.

A post shared by Marquee Singapore (@marqueesingapore)

A founding member of Swedish House Mafia and the creative force behind classics including 'Don't You Worry Child', 'Save the World', and 'I Found U', the four-time Grammy nominee has spent decades defining modern electronic music. From Tomorrowland and Ultra to EDC, Axwell's euphoric blend of melodic house and explosive drops continues to captivate audiences around the world, making this one of the month's most anticipated headline shows.

The celebrations continue on Saturday, 15 August, as Jai Wolf brings his cinematic soundscapes to Singapore. Widely celebrated for blending indie influences with emotionally charged electronic production, the producer has built a devoted following through releases like the RIAA Gold-certified 'Indian Summer' and his acclaimed debut album The Cure to Loneliness. With more than 500 million streams and performances across some of the world's biggest festivals, Jai Wolf's soaring melodies, organic textures, and immersive live sets promise a night unlike any other.

From dominating the stages of Tomorrowland, EDC Las Vegas, Ultra, and Creamfields to earning more than 20 Beatport No. 1 records, Ben Nicky continues to push boundaries with every performance. Expect an explosive journey packed with massive drops, euphoric melodies, and relentless energy from start to finish.

Closing out the month on Friday, 28 August, progressive house pioneer Nicky Romero returns for another unforgettable night. From the enduring success of 'Toulouse' to his iconic collaboration with Avicii, 'I Could Be The One', Romero has spent more than a decade shaping the sound of modern electronic music. A favourite on the world's biggest festival stages including Tomorrowland, Ultra Music Festival, and EDC, his signature blend of soaring melodies and festival-ready drops continues to unite dancefloors around the globe. Expect hands-in-the-air moments as one of electronic music's most influential names closes August in spectacular fashion.

items.body: Improvised free music recording develops around some recurring patterns: the single event in which musicians group, play and then disperse – the recording freezes a moment in time; the long term association – each recording a moment in a sequence sometimes with the risk of developing idioms, of creating a comfort zone at the expense of creative freedom; or a core of frequent collaborators meet a guest / guests - in this case the embryo of an idiom is here but it is tested and mutated by the newcomers. Forced to Feel offers still another possibility being recorded after the group has “already tested its chemistry on stage (…) at a moment of deepened trust and heightened risk, refining a shared language forged in performance and now pushed further in the studio” (linear notes). What I understand is that they are on their way to create an idiom but are still willing to experiment and take risks… their language is still a virus. Eyal Maoz (electric guitar), Piero Bittolo Bon (alto and baritone sax, shakuhachi, electronics), and Zeno De Rossi (drums, bells) all come to this meeting from different directions with Bittolo Bon and De Rossi having played together many times in many different contexts, and the results are intense. A meaningful use of electronics, a sort of underground groove that flows into this sonic universe, splinters of melody scattered into the noise. In the opening piece, Renato’s 'Arcade,' a set of electronic sounds coming directly from a 1980s arcade creates a foundation on which De Rossi builds his texture and Maoz and Bittolo Bon display their fragments of melodies. Music then evolves into a more pensive mood in 'Invoking the Ancestors' - the guitar provides a net of arpeggios and fragmented melodies while percussions, bells and electronics create a field for the alto sax to play a eerie song that dissolves into itself. In 'Nervous Butterflies' a quasi unison of electronics, sax and guitar open the piece developing a swarm of circular motives that evolve one into the other with the addition of the percussion. Something like a jazz-rock guitar emerges over a riff just to develop into angular sounds that seem nostalgic of other times. The drum than brings the sax into a jazzy atmosphere that seems to freeze into the end. 'Moon Hovering' builds on an obsessive percussive patterns and offers the possibility to mark the essential contribution that De Rossi offers to the trio creating a unifying but open and volatile design that enriches sense of global improvisation. The same may be true for 'Part Hypnosis' where the three musicians seem to find a place of their own. The baritone sax develops an obsessive melody in 'Flickering Wings,' this slowly changes into a deconstructed blues, sometimes some electronic noise adds an ironic note to prepare the finale with De Rossi again in evidence. 'Pull Me into the Blue Water' contains all of the elements presented so far with the addition of the shakuhachi flute that adds rarefaction to the mix. The guitar reacts with dreamy sonorities, the drum marks its path with a sense of necessity. That’s it. After many listening sessions, I feel that all of the fragments, the different sounds, the different attitudes gather into sonic nebulas each with its distinctive features but with an overall inner coherence. Undetermined and yet beautiful. You can listen to and download the digital album on bandcamp. forced to feel by Eyal Maoz, Piero Bittolo Bon & Zeno de Rossi Email This BlogThis! items.body: Label: Self released, 2026 Personnel - Gon Muruaga: electric guitar; Camila Nebbia: tenor saxophone; Jonathan Bäckström: double bass; Teemu Mustonen: drums. Gon Muruaga is an Argentinian guitarist and composer based in Helsinki, Finland. Unafraid of taking risks, Muruaga plays with open forms and fragmentation in a mix of aural explosions and quietly composed atmospheres, joining forces with fellow countrywoman Camila Nebbia on saxophone (a prominent figure in the free-improvisation scene) and the Finnish rhythm section of bassist Jonathan Bäckström and drummer Teemu Mustonen. Freefalling Latitude opens with “ Latifall ”, where Nebbia’s tenor descriptions trace geometric figures and sharp angles. Loose drums and bold guitar accompaniment support her unconditionally, while the bass enters late yet confidently. Muruaga pushes the electronic side of his instrument to the fore, employing delay effects while exploring skronky, clustered sounds. “ Fogradient ” has ethereal guitar waves contributing to the initial ambient texture, yet we can hear Bäckström’s bass lines pulsating in the background. There’s uncertainty within a spatial mist and formless void, but things gradually build toward a roaring climax. This alternation between rumination and eruption is a constant throughout. If “ Gyroslip ” features jarring, rusty guitar attacks, swift saxophone runs, and a lumpy, tribal-like groove underneath, “ Paralaxial ” and “ Isoplex ” investigate balmy sonic possibilities, whether through finespun percussion and unyielding yet mysterious harmonic contours or saxophone overtones and non-abrasive atmospheric friction. These are musicians who listen closely to one another, and “ Nebulode ” brings them together to unearth new sounds as part of the quartet’s exploratory aesthetic. Out of a maze of fragmentation, the band finds a raw connection through clattering percussion and inharmonic collisions. Its wry experimental vision remains engaging, keeping our ears wide open. Curiously, there’s something invigorating about this quartet, but also the lingering feeling that it is capable of achieving even more. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Latifall ► 04 - Gyroslip ► 05 - Nebulode

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar.
Vanishment
contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina�s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice.
The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette.

The stoic and twangy �Don�t Fault the Stars for Falling� could have been a Dolly Parton tune.

Hunt was a famed orator, a man on the side of the people, able to stir and inspire with his voice. Although the gathering was peaceful, the size of the crowd terrified the magistrates, who panicked and imagined an uprising. They sent in half-trained dragoons and the cavalry, who rode down, slashed and killed without compunction or compassion. In the end, 18 died and up to 700 were wounded. It was a stain on the nation, an outrage; prompting Percy Shelley, one of the poetic giants of the age, to write The Masque of Anarchy , with its famous lines: �Rise like Lions after slumber / in unvanquishable number / She your chains to earth like dew / Which in sleep had fallen on you / Ye are many - they are few.� Peterloo, as people called it, remains one of the seminal events in English working-class history, one that Sean Cooney of the Young 'Uns has revisited for this album of original songs, which is lavishly presented in a book with contemporary letters, political cartoons and illustrations to create a multimedia event. It�s ambitious, no doubt about that, and he�s selected some great talent to help � guitarist Sam Carter, the almost ubiquitous fiddler/singer Eliza Carthy, Ben Nicholls supplying background and texture on various instruments, and the Lancashire industrial ballad singer Jennifer Reid, who doubles as narrator. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid For a small ensemble, they make a powerful noise. The songs capture the feel of the day; the anticipation and excitement at the summer gathering, the joy that turns to terror and flight as the troops charge, then the bitter, mournful aftermath, voiced some powerful melodies and very well-chosen images. As a writer, Cooney often focuses on the personal in the small tales of people like �Sam Bamford� and �Mary Fildes,� while the three short pieces that comprise �The Monkey Rides The Mare� capture the bluster and arrogance of the soldiers. Peter's Field by Sean Cooney, Eliza Carthy, Sam Carter, Jennifer Reid Cooney is a persuasive singer, and on this heartfelt project, he puts plenty of emotion into his voice. Having two other outstanding vocalists alongside him makes for a wonderful triple threat. In these days when governments across the world are cracking down on protest, this stands as a sobering and very timely reminder. It�s a history lesson, yes, but the detail of the history stays in the book, while the music creates a set of songs that will resonate and remain for a long time. Find the artist online. items.body:
Live at Rockpalast 1999
documents a command performance at the Loreley open-air amphitheater by Malcolm �Mac� Rebennack Jr., aka Dr. John. Rockpalast is a live-music TV show broadcast since 1974 by Westdeutscher Rundfunk (WDR), the archival source for this CD-DVD package, and coincidentally a remarkable cultural institution on its own terms.
Taped at the height of Dr. John�s international popularity, backing the singer-pianist-guitarist are New Orleans stalwarts Bobby Broom (guitar), David Barard (bass), and Herman Ernest (drums), a tight quartet that projects authority and engages the crowd from start to close.
A striking UNESCO-designated World Heritage Site set, the Loreley is a slate pinnacle on a mythic horseshoe bend of the Rhine River, memorializing an enduring German literary legend both tragic and romantic. The setting is thus well-suited for Mac�s mystical spirit and lyrical style. By this stage of his career, he characterized his live show as a Mardi Gras revue with a mix of New Orleans standards and some of his most recognizable compositions.
Hence, he opens with the NOLA classic �Iko, Iko,� a half-sung, half-chanted celebration of community participation in the renowned Mardi Gras second-line street procession. Then comes the in-your-face boast �Qualified,� wherein the singer warns, �I got the power to control / I can see clean through you, blind mole / I want to tell you now, I'm qualified / You know that I'm qualified.�
Any Dr. John fan will recognize �I Walk on Guilded Splinters,� a moody, percussively insistent, foreboding expression of the Night Tripper�s immersion in �funknology� (his term), gris-gris herbology, and hoodoo incantation, punctuated with jungle growls and cries, a loopy, spooky slide whistle, and an extended psych-guitar solo: �Walk thru the fire / Fly thru the smoke / See my enemy / At the end of dey rope.�
Every piece in this well- honed set deserves considertion. Although Dr John lived for many years in Los Angeles and New York, his enduring hometown connection shows in the fond inclusion of his own �Sweet Home New Orleans� and �Goin� Back to New Orleans,� and he nods to a key influence with a funky rendering of Duke Ellington�s �I'm Gonna Go Fishin�.� Among other gems are Mac�s Top�10 hit �Right Place, Wrong Time,� and the instantly recognizable closer, Earl King�s �Big Chief,� another Mardi Gras burner.
Regarding his live performance approach, per the notes, �I always play a little bit of everything. I think that�s what music�s about: a little bit of somethin� old, somethin� in the middle, somethin� new, and somethin� as yet uncreated.�
Dr John's�s longtime fans will welcome this archival gem, which also is a solid introduction for any late comers to the party. Surmounting the barriers of language and culture, the power of
At the Rockpalast
is also evident in the enthusiastic audience response. As he declares, �If you�re gonna get off on somethin� you don�t need to know nothin� about it. Music is a universal language.�

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items.body: Editor's note: When this set of recordings came to me, I was at a loss as to how to share it. It's not music, in any traditional sense (although there is some freestyle rapping), and a 'review' of such an artifact of reality seems superfluous to the content. Instead, I asked sound recordist Ian Brennan if I could simply use his own brief commentary and the recordings he made on the street in Chicago. Twenty-five people afflicted by gun violence participated, many from the very block we�d setup on. Many neighbors were pulled-in spontaneously. Almost every one in the community had been impacted by violence somehow� both on the receiving and the inflicting end, and many both. One woman had just come from a memorial service, another was on her way. That�s how far-reaching the violence. Almost no one went untouched. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors By chance, we convened on the day that Trump ordered the deployment of the National Guard to the city. The recording took place on the front porch of the leader's ninety-four-year-old grandmother's house�right in the heart of the ��hood,� beneath the Midway Airport�s landing path. A pair of stray pitfalls stalked the block. But the grandmother warned not of gunshots, but the mosquitoes in her yard. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors We were in a section of town that one man defined as �the forgotten parts.� Just a short jaunt from the designer clothes shops and posh hotels of the city�s Magnificent Mile, the Southside spawned such legendary Blues artists as Muddy Waters, Willie Dixon, and Howlin� Wolf. Jazz musicians like Lionel Hampton and even Benny Goodman, hailed from nearby. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors The participants ranged in age from seventeen to sixty-seven, but the pattern held true. The person who�d asserted �you�ll really want to hear my story,� was the least compelling. The reluctant, the most moving. One elder�s tough facade broke down as she shared how she�d lost both her sons. She tearfully apologized, �I�m sorry. I�m sorry. I�m sorry.� But she had nothing to be sorry for. Society is the one that owes the apology� for the staggering statistical inequities of which no reasonable defense can be made. The Forgotten Parts by Chicago Gunfire Survivors Editor's note: The full set of recordings are available on Bandcamp. Any profits from this project will be donated to Cure Violence Global , who states that their mission is "advancing an evidence-based health approach to end violence globally." When I asked him about the background sounds, producer Ian Brennan added, "No music is added. It�s all sounds from the source environment. I also ran loops/drones on a different track in the background as they spoke, and when they ended up being incidentally/somewhat magically/eerily synchronous, that is what was used for a few pieces with 'accompaniment' like some of the rap freestyles."
